subject: Banking
title: M-Pesa: Banking Without Banks
description: A fast breakdown of M-Pesa: Banking Without Banks for builders.

hook.text: M-Pesa lets 50 million Kenyans send money by text message. No bank account, no internet, just a basic phone.

buildup.text: Launched by Safaricom in 2007, M-Pesa uses a network of local agents.

discovery.text: M-Pesa processes $300 billion annually, moving 50% of Kenya's GDP via mobile phones where most people are unbanked.

twist.text: M-Pesa lifted 2% of Kenyan households out of extreme poverty.

climax.text: M-Pesa proved that phones can replace banks in places banks never went.

punchline.text: 50 million users. $300 billion processed. Banking by text message.

quiz.question: How does M-Pesa work?
options: Via text messages and a network of local cash agents

details.summary: M-Pesa launched in Kenya in 2007 as a mobile phone-based money transfer service that became the first massively successful mobile money system, bringing financial services to millions who had never had a bank account.
details.whyItMatters: M-Pesa proved that financial inclusion does not require banks. A telecom company with a network of small agents accomplished what traditional banks never could, lifting millions out of extreme poverty through financial access.
takeaways: M-Pesa has over 51 million active users across multiple African countries
It uses simple SMS technology that works on basic feature phones
Research estimates M-Pesa lifted 2 percent of Kenyan households out of poverty

faq.question: How did M-Pesa succeed where banks failed?
faq.answer: Banks required branches, documentation, and minimum balances that excluded most Kenyans. M-Pesa used existing mobile phone networks and a network of small shop agents. Customers only needed a basic phone and national ID to start transacting.

faq.question: Is M-Pesa still relevant with smartphone banking apps?
faq.answer: M-Pesa remains dominant in East Africa because it works on basic feature phones without internet access. It has also evolved to include savings, loans, and international transfers, maintaining relevance even as smartphones spread.
